reasoning.Student A:
Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, truthful reporting is a dominant strategy: no possible misrepresentation of my preferences can yield a strictly better assignment regardless of how others rank schools. My true preference ordering is z > w > y > x, and I should therefore submit that ranking.

Although I have highest priority at w and y (w:1, y:1) and lower priority at z (z:2) and x (x:2), and many others favor y > x > w > z, these facts do not change the dominant strategy. Trying to rank a less-preferred school higher to game priorities cannot improve my outcome under a strategy-proof mechanism and may only risk getting a worse assignment. Thus I will report my true preferences.
reasoning.Student B:
The mechanism is strategy-proof, so truthful reporting is a dominant strategy: no ranking I submit can give me a better outcome than listing my true preferences, regardless of what others do.

My true preference ordering is z > x > w > y. I also have top priority (1) at x and z and lower priority (2) at w and y. Many other applicants favor y, and I have only priority 2 at y, so even if I wanted to try to "game" by ranking y higher to increase chances there, the strategy-proof property ensures that misrepresenting preferences cannot improve my final assignment. Thus I should and will rank schools honestly in the order z, x, w, y.

Although many applicants favor y and my priorities at y and z are relatively low (priority 4), attempting to manipulate by ranking a more attainable school higher would not improve my outcome under a strategy-proof mechanism. Therefore you should submit your true preference order.
